01

A small visual experiment

The sunset style test

First, prove the look in a small story.

I started with an ordinary character and a deliberately modest problem: he is late for watching the sunset. That gave me a reason to test a close-up, a walk and a change of light without needing a large cast or a factual explanation.

The joke is the mismatch between his urgency and his very easy job. The final light change supplies the payoff. This is an original fictional premise, so its purpose was visual calibration.

How I turned the idea into shots

The opening establishes his deadpan face and the deadline. At about 3.53 seconds, the camera follows his walk. At about 6.63 seconds, the scene turns golden and his expression relaxes. Those three beats exercise the shared renderer’s most important features in just 10.2 seconds.

What the early renders taught me

I refined the cap brim and contour weight, adjusted the walk stride for the viewing angle, and kept the sunset shadows blue-violet instead of letting the whole image become orange-brown. The character drawing sits on a lit plane in the 3D town, which helps the figure belong in the scene.

The rendering integration also needed a repair: the post-processing chain had to be ready before a frame was captured. I assembled it synchronously and waited for the GPU to finish, avoiding blank captures from an initialization race.

02

A science explanation

The Magnet That Fell in Slow Motion

Choose a paradox that can be demonstrated.

For the first full minute, I chose a magnet falling slowly through copper. The hook is immediately visible: a material that does not attract the magnet like iron still slows its fall. One repeated action can carry a control experiment, an explanation and a final comparison.

The narration develops that question in steps: an ordinary metal cylinder falls quickly; the magnet falls slowly; changing magnetic flux drives currents; the currents produce a braking force; a longitudinal slit weakens that brake. The ending returns to the idea of breaking a circuit.

Let the lighting carry the explanation

I staged the demonstration in the painted town and moved into labeled X-ray views for the mechanism. Blue light marks the explanation; warmer light returns for the slit and comparison. Yellow circulation markers, blue field curves and force arrows make the invisible process readable.

What I verified

  • A conducting copper tube can slow a falling magnet through induced currents and energy dissipation. Levin, da Silveira and Rizzato.
  • A slit reduces braking; it does not eliminate all currents or guarantee free fall. University of Sydney activity.
  • The colored fields, fall speeds and heat particles are illustrations, not numerical measurements. Full source and illustration notes.

What I corrected in review

I clarified the transparent views versus the physical slit, improved magnet visibility, kept the small residual-current loops on intact copper, corrected the final framing and preserved clearance through the tube. Both illustrated braking forces point upward.

“the science one focusses too much on the magnet.”
Your feedback after the science short

The close views made the mechanism clear, but gave the prop most of the attention. Your feedback changed the next brief: choose a story whose decisions and consequences can be shown through people.

03

A story carried by people

The Captain’s Hat — Robert Smalls

Make the people carry the story.

I chose Robert Smalls’s 1862 escape because it contains decisions, cooperation, disguise, suspense and a reunion. It also gives the story a strong final turn: his later service in Congress. The crew and family supply the emotional stakes; the ship supplies the setting.

The opening introduces Smalls in disguise. The story then follows the planning, the white officers’ departure, the families boarding, the passage past the forts, the white sheet, the Union handover and the reunion. A clear “Years later” transition takes the narration into his political life.

Translate the feedback into animation choices

I added directed poses for both arms: steering, whispering, pointing, pulling a signal cord, folding the arms, embracing, waving and holding a resolved stance. Walks use side drawings. Expressions, blinks and small head movements keep attention on the cast, while camera movements stay gentle.

The shot review led to concrete fixes: track the departing officer, widen the family and handover views, keep the child’s face free of structural lines, make the white sheet visible beside the people, and remove a foreground hat that competed with Smalls in the epilogue. Period straw hats and kepis replaced more contemporary-looking caps.

Let the evidence change the staging

  • Smalls imitates the captain’s pose while another freedom seeker steers; women and children remain concealed during the fort passage. National Park Service.
  • The narration says “parts of five terms” in the House, matching the more precise congressional biography. U.S. House of Representatives.
  • I omitted disputed exact passenger counts and invented attributed dialogue. Faces, room layouts and specific reactions are staged reconstruction. Full historical sources and limits.

Keep the pace without rushing the voice

The final script contains 196 words. I shortened 11.56 seconds of long pauses outside the recognized word boundaries, then used pitch-preserving time compression at about 1.134×. Speech ends at 59.6 seconds; the sound bed finishes the minute. Footsteps were aligned to the actual walk contacts, and the corrected soundtrack was added without re-encoding the picture.

The production method shared by all three.

“Learning the style” meant translating references into reusable rules for drawing, lighting, composition and timing. Each film is a coded Three.js scene rendered through Remotion. Story-specific geometry and acting sit on top of the shared visual system.

  1. Choose the questionA small deadline, an apparent contradiction, or a human decision with clear stakes.
  2. Check the storySeparate a fictional premise from claims that need scientific or historical evidence.
  3. Write to the durationBuild a hook, escalation and payoff; trim material that cannot be staged clearly.
  4. Make the voiceGenerate original narration, align its words and establish the actual time budget.
  5. Stage the actionPlace characters, props and cameras around the narrated beats.
  6. Review representative framesFix framing, contours, colors, depth and anything crossing a face.
  7. Build the soundSynthesize original music and effects, duck the music under speech and align the cues.
  8. Render and verifyExport the frames, check the file, inspect samples and test playback.

What makes the look cohere

Simple expressive faces, small bodies and thin limbs sit in richer painted scenery. The figures receive scene lighting. Plum contours, warm highlights, cool shadows, selective focus and restrained camera movement tie the layers together.

The same caption treatment appears throughout: bold white words, a dark outline and hard changes at spoken word starts. The narrator is the ElevenLabs Asher James library voice. Scribe supplied word timings, which I edited or remapped to match the final audio. The music and effects were synthesized locally with Python.

Why timing comes before polish

Word times determine when a reaction, gesture, light change or camera move should happen. Captions come from that same timing data. The shared clock keeps the story, acting and sound in agreement.

For the history episode, shortening pauses required remapping the caption times as well. The final footstep correction also required a new soundtrack, while the video stream could be preserved.

Technical implementation and production notes

The shared compositor runs the scene, world ink, lens prepass, lens main pass, bloom, neutral tone mapping and grading in a controlled order. The final output uses a 1,080 × 1,920 composition rendered at 4/3 scale, producing 1,440 × 2,560 pixels at 30 fps.

Scene + character drawings → Three.js → ink → lens prepass → lens main pass → bloom + tone map + grade → captions + audio → H.264 / AAC
  • Shared rendering and sound workflow.
  • Sunset production notes.
  • Science production notes.
  • History production notes.
  • Retained source-code license notice.

What I would carry forward

Start the next story by naming the person making the decision and the visible action that expresses it. Keep the scientific or historical evidence precise, but let framing, reactions and interactions decide where the viewer looks. The main lesson across these three films is that technical consistency and attention are separate creative problems.

Automated checks

Every exported frame was decoded and inspected at reduced resolution for scene content, black or white frames, and frozen spans of 12 frames or longer. The checks also covered dimensions, frame rate, duration, caption timing and audio levels. Both full-minute episodes have explicit caption-to-script agreement checks.

Visual and playback checks

Representative frames were inspected during iteration and after export. The two full-minute videos were played to the end in a browser without a media error. These checks support delivery; they do not amount to a complete human audiovisual audit or a claim that the original reference channel’s renderer has been reproduced exactly.
